source.title: Beyond a Bag of Features: Set-Level Instability in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Nikolai Bolik; Lennart Stöpler; Artur Andrzejak

page_placements.theme: Contextual, temporal and perturbation sensitivity of SAE codes

record.tranche_reason: The study uses toy and natural-language SAE signature comparisons to test set-level compositional consistency, rather than measuring the original superposition geometry. Its controlled semantic-refinement experiments directly test whether SAE latent sets behave as stable compositional units.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports category-boundary, typicality, and natural-text clustering results. These evaluate semantic similarity, but do not directly test whether features overlap across dimensions, whether neurons share features due to capacity pressure, or whether SAE latents recover canonical model features. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether active SAE latent sets compose as stable bag-of-features units. Toy SAEs are trained on synthetic superposed features, and LLM SAE signatures are compared under adjective refinement. Its own numbers show 20–60% of noun latents lost when compatible adjectives are added, which argues that V5's 'stable units' reading needs restating. T5 fits better than T2: the study does not revisit the original superposition question but gives results that one version is partial.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely correct. Add that SAE set similarities do not match human category boundaries or typicality better than dense representations, and instead track model-internal similarity. The authors conclude that SAE features do not compose via simple bag-of-features semantics outside idealised settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures SAE active-set overlap and signature changes under synthetic feature composition and adjective-modified prompts, rather than reproducing the original superposition experiments' geometry and feature-weighting analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Lost-latent rates vary with the number of added adjectives and model depth; upstream activity and pre-activation patterns vary by model family and layer. Toy union consistency varies with SAE width and the number of ground-truth features.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE signature Jaccard similarity does not recover human category boundaries (peak AMI often below dense cosine) or within-category typicality (Spearman around zero). It tracks dense residual-stream similarity instead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent-set similarity aligns with human conceptual structure no better than dense representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Lost latents are often active upstream (about 60% mid-layer for Gemma, about 40% for Llama), and on the noun position they are mostly near-threshold rather than negative. Mistral is the exception, with mostly negative pre-activations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Signature instability under refinement is partly position-local and subthreshold rather than active suppression.

fits_no_version.finding: Random positive steering along SAE decoder directions induces loss rates comparable to real prompts in some layers. It does not match the layerwise trend, and it differs across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interference among superposed latent directions partly but not fully explains SAE signature loss.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and the browser will be released upon acceptance
record.problems: Detailed layer- and variant-specific results are largely presented in figures; the text gives qualitative summaries rather than exact values for many of them. The naturalistic compositionality experiment tests adjective modification of nouns, and the authors note that this may not generalize to other forms of semantic refinement.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed model-, SAE-variant-, and layer-specific curves in Figures 20–29 and 31–38 are not transcribed individually; the rows above capture the numerical or explicit aggregate trends stated in the text. Category-boundary and typicality results were left out because they do not directly test the listed versions' claims about superposition or SAE feature recovery.

untested.parts: Completeness and canonicality of SAE features are not tested. This includes recovery of ground-truth directions in the toy, and cross-seed or cross-width canonical units. Only set-level compositional consistency under adjective refinement is tested.
The toy activations are built as superpositions by design. The study does not test whether networks learn overlapping near-orthogonal storage, sparsity-dependent transitions, or geometry.
Whether SAEs recover the model's sparse features is not measured. The natural-text clustering is qualitative only.
Not tested. Multidimensional features are discussed only in related work.

missing.what: Lost-latent trends are broadly consistent across SAE families, including Matryoshka SAEs designed against absorption, which argues against absorption as the main cause. This is a robustness result for the V5 challenge.
Stepwise lost-latent rates stay substantial across consecutive refinements, with the largest drop from t0 to t1.
The toy N=70 union-consistency result shown in the main text.

record.verdict_notes: The toy studies serve as the authors' validation that set-level analysis is meaningful. They test union consistency of SAE codes on activations constructed as superpositions, not ground-truth recovery. The challenge to V5 concerns compositional stability of active latent sets, not completeness or canonicality; it rests on one refinement type (adjective plus noun) and a single fixed template. TopK SAEs (GPT-2, Llama) cannot satisfy union by construction, so cross-model loss for those models partly reflects architecture.

versions.untested_parts: The toy experiments test SAE signature union consistency, not whether a network stores excess sparse features as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions or whether direction geometry changes with feature sparsity or importance.
The paper does not test whether neurons become polysemantic because features compete for neuron capacity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The paper does not test other causes of polysemantic neurons.
The paper analyzes SAE signatures but does not test whether features are distributed across neurons or whether SAEs recover the model's underlying features.
The experiments test set-level compositional consistency and stability under adjective refinement, not whether SAE features are complete or canonical units in every sense.
The study does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: LRH-aligned toy model with directions sampled from Gemma Scope decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained SAEs on synthetic activations made from selected near-orthogonal decoder directions and evaluated union consistency.
rows.measure: Jaccard, recall, and precision for union consistency
rows.baseline: Expected union of the two single-feature signatures
rows.value: Union consistency is typically recovered for sufficiently wide SAEs; metrics can also be high in the strongly compressed regime, while the strongest failure is around SAE width 200 and becomes more pronounced as N increases.
rows.uncertainty: One standard deviation across three random seeds is shown in the figure; numerical values not stated in text.
rows.note: The authors caution that high scores in the severely capacity-limited regime may reflect inputs collapsing onto coarse shared latent patterns, not faithful resolution of individual directions.
rows.check: The state is fine. High scores at very narrow widths are flagged by the authors as possible collapse onto coarse shared latents, not faithful resolution.

rows.subject: Gemma 3 270M
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of latents active for the noun-only prompt that become inactive on the noun token after adding compatible adjectives.
rows.value: Typically between 20% and 60%; increases with k and often with model depth.
rows.uncertainty: Dataset means with one-standard-deviation bands are shown in Figure 4; numerical uncertainty values not stated in text.
rows.note: This is the main-text result for adjective refinement; the expected union-of-properties behavior would largely preserve the base noun latents.
rows.check: The state should be absent, not reversed. Expected preservation of base-noun latents fails, since 20–60% are lost, but no opposite effect is shown. Signatures are not disjoint.

rows.subject: Gemma 3 270M
rows.operation_detail: Probed upstream residual-stream states with the layer-specific SAE to determine whether latents lost at the noun position had been active earlier.

conditions.value: full phrase; inset also checks noun positions only

rows.measure: Fraction of lost latents previously active upstream
rows.baseline: Latents lost on the noun signature at layer ℓ
rows.value: Low in early layers, rises to roughly 60% in middle layers, then decreases in later layers.
rows.uncertainty: Dataset means with one-standard-deviation bands are shown in Figure 4; numerical uncertainty values not stated in text.
rows.note: The noun-only upstream curve closely agrees with the full-sequence curve.
rows.check: This is a mechanism diagnostic: whether lost latents were active upstream. It does not measure stability or composition of SAE units, but it qualifies how to read r9.

rows.subject: Gemma 3 270M
rows.operation_detail: Classified pre-activations of previously active but subsequently lost latents at the layer where loss was measured.

conditions.value: noun position; full phrase also analyzed

rows.value: On the noun signature, around 80% are near-zero, with only few negative latents; over the full phrase the negative fraction is typically 10%–20%.
rows.uncertainty: Dataset means with one-standard-deviation bands are shown in Figure 4; numerical uncertainty values not stated in text.
rows.note: This indicates that many lost latents are weakly aligned at the noun position rather than strongly suppressed.
rows.check: This is a pre-activation regime classification of lost latents. It is a mechanism diagnostic, not a measure of the version's effect.

rows.subject: All investigated models (authors' cross-model summary)
rows.operation_detail: Measured lost-latent rates under adjective refinement across available layers and SAE variants.

conditions.value: cross-model qualitative summary in Appendix E.2

rows.measure: Change in lost-latent rate with number of added adjectives
rows.value: The lost-latent rate increases by roughly 20 percent over the five investigated construction steps; the increase is less pronounced beyond k = 2.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a shared observation across investigated models.
rows.check: Not reversed: the loss of base latents grows with k (about +20% over five steps). GPT-2 Small and Llama 3.1 8B use TopK-style SAEs, which the authors say structurally cannot satisfy the union property (footnote 5). Some loss in those models is therefore forced by the architecture.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly argues that naturalistic SAE signatures violate simple bag-of-features composition, qualifying the stability aspect of V5.
